blocks.x: Who is at the La Vida with you? You were talking about that.

Oh, I mentioned the fellow that was at the La Vida with me already. Such as Lee Collins, uh, John Marrero, Simon Marrero, uh, Roy Evans was there with me on drums, and Alfred William on drums, and, uh, David Jones on tennis sax, Rubichaud on piano.
Trombone, did you?
Jim Robinson on trombone. None of that.
Yeah, we got it, right? Now, when did you leave the La Vida? What year? Do you remember that?

Oh, I left the La Vida somewhere around, uh, I was around, uh, I was around 27, I think. No. I was around, uh, I was around, uh, 29 to 30, I got La Vida. Because, uh, I got to La Vida to organize a band, and was playing at the, at that time they called it the Golden Dragon, but that was the, the story. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. And then, there to the Pelican. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. How many years were you at the La Vida?
Uh-huh. I was actually at La Vida from, uh, around 26. Uh-huh. Until around 30. So, uh, then who did you have at the Pelican and the Golden Dragon?
Oh, I had a pretty large orchestra here, I told you yesterday.
The Louisiana Shakespeare. Yeah. Uh-huh. That bunch. I had that bunch together there then.
Who was your bass player with that band?
Kimball. Old man Kimball.
I was trying to remember his name, but I'll check on that.
You might know his son, he used to, he's a left-handed guitar, used to play with, uh, Celestine. He plays, uh.
He plays bass now. Bass now.
Yeah, he's a bass viola player.
Well, it's his daddy then. That's what I wanted to get straight.

Yeah, his daddy. Uh-huh. Uh. Well, after I left, uh, Pelican, I left here and went to St. Louis. Worked at the Democratic Club there. Uh-huh. Under a fellow by the name of Hawkins. At the Democratic Club at that time. My Bobby Gordon up there, it was through our, uh, Charlie Chris. Used to work with, with Faith Morgan. He played trumpet and he played, uh, the accordion. Oh. He's dead now, a fellow. Uh, up there I had, uh, I can't remember this guy's name. I don't remember one man's name up there. Was playing with us too. I remember a fellow called Cabbage playing, uh, tenor saxophone. Another boy they called, uh, Bubba, I think they called him. This drummer used to be on the boobah seat. Uh, played at Democratic Club for about 89 months. Maybe, probably a year I played at Democratic Club. And then I left there and went down to 34 East Market. Played a fellow down there, that Italian name, Sam. I played there for, until I got sick. I was there about six months, seven months. Matter of fact, that's the last place I seen Guy Kelly. He was with, uh, uh, Walter Barnes' band. Got burned up in Natchez there. Uh-huh. He was with that band. He come down and stopped in St. Louis there. As a matter of fact, they played somewhere near St. Louis, and on the way back to Chicago, they stopped there. And somebody told them I was at, uh, 34 East Market down there. And they come down there, the whole band come down there. I was playing with a fellow by the name of Joe, Jay Guston, and he was a nice arranger, and he was a piano player. And they had ten pieces in there every night.
Uh-huh.
That's where I made, met Julius and Pillars out of St. Louis. They were at that, uh, Club Plantation, I think, that's the name of the place they were playing.
Did they have many New Orleans grounds up there with those phones?

No. Uh, Gishard, he's from here, but he was playing with another band on the name of Eddie. Eddie something they was playing. He's a saxophone player too, a how-to player. And he had a brother, a dead shawty, played bass, but I think the young ones did the bass play. I think he died. I had a fellow out at, uh, Shreveport with, uh, Goldstone's band. I played a lot of, a lot of, a lot of Tramon too. A little skinny fella. I forget his name too. Fine Tramon player. I only had a guy playing trumpet there, second trumpet. Called him Sleepy. He'd come down here with fate too. That guy wouldn't play nothing but second trumpet. He wouldn't play nothing. And Guy Kelly coming in that night, and Guy and I played a number two with us. And this fella had been sitting up there playing like that for seven to eight months. And Guy came in there and played so much trumpet, man. He'd come in there and played so much trumpet, man. This guy got up and washed Guy out, man. He washed him out. Broke up the house, man. We all had to stop and look at him. Didn't know he was sitting back there for eight or nine months. He didn't play nothing but second. Strictly music. Didn't try to get off at all, you know. Man, all of a sudden he came out that blowing. Well, I stayed at that place until I got sick. Got sick around. 38, 39. I stayed in Homer Phillip Hospital there in St. Louis for three years. And I was sitting back in the back. And I was sitting back in the back. And I was sitting back in the back. And I was sitting back in the back. And I was sitting back in the back. I was sitting back in the back. I was sitting back in the back. I went back down to my job. I had a fellow from here. I died from here. I had a place in Springfield, Illinois. I came up and asked me to come up there and wait for him. I taken six pieces and went up there. Was it six? Five or six. I was a drummer, piano, saxophone. I didn't have no trumpet. That's about all I had. Three pieces. I had two girls singing. Me to five. Two girls were singing.
What were the names of the other people?
No.
You don't know? I can't remember. They were New Orleans people?

No. One of the boys was from Springfield. His name was Johnny. Johnny something. He was the drummer. I had a little fellow from Los Angeles, California playing piano. I can't think of his name right off. But he was a wonderful piano player. He got his hands with Sue Lily. He had to take this hard paper like that and wrap it around his sandwich with rubber to make it sound. Rubber to make it make tense on the piano. The only way he can make tense on the piano. The only way he can make tense on the piano. Put a piece of paper on his finger to make his finger long enough so he can make tense on the piano.
I heard of that.

Well, he had a little bit of air on the piano. But play. Ooh, he could play some piano. And never was sober. Never was sober. He stayed right there in the same hotel with us. He wake up in the morning and get drunk. Get drunk when he eat. Twelve o'clock he get drunk. Go to work he's drunk. Come from work he's drunk. But play. Never was late on the job. And never went to sleep. Never went to sleep. But he'd be drunk. Played everything you put in front of him and what you don't put in front of him he played. He was a wonderful guy. I remember one night him and the taxi cab driver after they'd taken us home. By the way, that's where I met Don Albert in Springfield. You didn't know him down here. You didn't know him down here, huh? Yeah, I know him down here. But I hadn't seen him in about three, four years. He had Alvin Alcorn with him then. And a drummer from around there used to call him Fat. He died up in Texas a couple years ago. He was playing with me when he left with me when he left with Don Albert in Springfield. And Alvin Alcorn was playing with me on the Pelican. And they left him with Don. What was a Pelican? What was a Pelican? I was on Gravy and Ramport. Just a big dance hall. One of the bigger dance halls was around here at that time. I remember when I first come here to New Orleans. These guys used to have a habit of stuff with stuff When they want you tricky on the bandstand, they let you get up there and blow your tops. And then the trumpet player would slip his trumpet out at ease. And knock off a number. Now you find it. Renee did me that out at the fairground. I was out there. I played five or six numbers. People all gathering around and staring. Carrying on and clapping and raising. And Renee slipped that trumpet in the air on me. And knocked off high society. I couldn't find no, no, no kind of way. And I know I had been playing with the, Fate on the jam sessions, Fate Marvel. Fate Marvel start a number and one sharp and run it all the way to the seven. And he'd come back, right back and start a number one flat and run all the way to seven flats. And I was in the jam session. But he never did lose me. But Renee lost me in high society. I was in the high society. I couldn't get in there nowhere in the world. I never did forget that either. Did you play much with Renee? Oh yeah, I played a lot with Renee. As a matter of fact, he tried all kinds of ways to get me to join his band. I wouldn't leave Tom Alvin. He had a nice, he had a nice, uh, clarinet player with him. A fellow by the name of Zeb. Playing clarinet with him.
Is he still alive, Zeb?

No, Zeb's dead. The guy I really liked to hear play clarinet. He played such a sweet clarinet. It was, uh, a fellow by the name of Watson. Used to play with Sam Morgan. I used to like to hear him play clarinet. And he used to like to hear me play. Because the OAC, he wanted me to blow. And I, you know, I'd just rather hear him play than play myself. He didn't make so much, but what he made was so pretty and clean. Real fine clarinet player. I went down to, uh, Pete Herman's. Played down there with, uh, Bebe Ridgely. Uh huh. At that time, I had, uh, John Porter on bass. Arthur Williams on drums. Shots on trumpet. Bebe on trombone. Uh, Emma Barrett on piano. Uh, it was old after.

I was playing clarinet. I was doing clarinet. And what about the name of Earl? His name was Earl Trusclair. He's the first man that ever showed me any finger on a saxophone. We alternated. He showed me my finger on the saxophone and I showed him his finger on the clarinet. And that's the only thing anybody ever showed me about a saxophone. Oh, no. Nobody never showed me nothing about a clarinet, but on the saxophone, that's the only fella ever showed me anything. He showed me how to finger it. And other than that, I didn't have any more. That's all I needed, you know, because if I learned how to finger it, I could learn how to play it. All I wanted to know how to finger it, you know. And we played, we stayed down there at Pete Harmon for, I guess, a year or something. That was right after Solistan the band. And then Baby Ridgely broke the band up. Who took Solistan's place when they

broke up? Oh, well, Solistan made up his own band. I mean, on the trumpet, when Ridgely. Shatz. Shatz. And was he playing with you at the Pete Hermans? Who, Shatz? Yeah, I forget who you said was there. Yeah, Shatz was on trumpet at Pete Hermans. Uh-huh. Mm-hmm. Okay, he was playing trumpet. What else? I was wondering about, uh, did you ever meet Charlie Parker around Kansas City or St. Louis or any of those places?
Charlie Parker? Mm-hmm. No, I don't think. Uh-uh. Yeah, I just, I just wondered if he was
coming up then in those years. No. Did you ever know him? No, I never know Charlie Parker. Somebody had just mentioned, you know, that he used to listen to you. Somebody told me that, you know.

He might have. He might have, but I, I, I didn't know anything about it because he used to have so many of these guys sit around and stand on the outside. Mm-hmm. They wouldn't show their face. They stand outside, they'd listen. I like, uh, this fellow, Earl Bostic. Mm-hmm. He didn't know him. But Bostic didn't care who seen him listening because he'd come in anywhere I'd be. And wouldn't blow up notes. All the horn he played wouldn't play a thing. But he'd stare. I don't care where I was playing. If he couldn't come in, they'd be outside. And he just kept on hanging around, hanging around, hanging around. When I did hear him play, I thought it was me playing. Edgar Sochi was the same thing. Uh, Wiggles, you know, Parnel? Mm-hmm. He was the same thing. All them just hung around, hung around. Joe Harris. Now, that was a firecrust, a nice punk player. He played with, uh, Earl Foster. You know him? I don't know. I can't play him. I must play him. He got a wonderful tone. And he played a lot of horns. A lot of horns, Joe Harris. He played a lot of horns. At least he was. I haven't heard him now in about five, six years because he got paralyzed and he can hardly walk unless he's walking with a stick. But I sent him at the, at the banquet. He didn't have no stick when I sent him at the banquet.
He was getting all fine. Um, yesterday we were talking about Earl Foster and some of the guys that used to work with him. Who did you mention?

Yeah, well I said he was playing with, uh, Kaiser. Oh yeah, Kaiser used to be with him. Yeah, they was at, uh, Cornell and, uh, Burgundy. They had a night, uh, jitney dance, taxi dance up there, upstairs. And they worked there for quite a number of years. Poor Earl used to sing until he sing himself to sleep. He fell asleep while he was singing? He fell asleep while he was playing the drums. I went up there many nights and played for hours or so before him let him sleep. Played drums for him. Go downstairs in his car and go to sleep. The only trouble about that, you could have stopped playing the drums though. Couldn't go get him out. No. He sent somebody for him. And you send somebody downstairs and they forget to tell him. Keep going. Yeah, that's one thing about the drum and the piano and the guitar. Of course, the piano stopped if you want. The guitar played, the guitar stopped, the piano played. But the drummer never did stop. The guitar played. And I hadn't flew with drums in quite a number of years and it would get you in your anchor, you know. You'd play so long and your anchor began to get swell up on it. And, uh, Earl never would come upstairs. Be down there snowing in that car. But he used to, Earl was a smart guy, you know. He'd play that music all night and drive that big old truck all day long. Pick it up, that pieceboard stuff. And bought him two, three homes like that. And he got money now.
Yeah, he was a smart guy.

Should have brought me a truck. Yeah. When I had a 50-year-old. I wasn't thinking about nothing like that. I had some, uh, a lot of good office to leave here when I was a young man. I still got a lot of telegrams around home there. Yeah. When I fooled around and got married and after I got married my first child was born. I wouldn't leave then. You know, I wouldn't go anywhere.
You want to save all those telegrams and letters, you know.
Yeah, I got them around home there somewhere in some, some of the drawers.
Yeah, we might, can make copies of them. You know, we got a camera to do that.
Oh yeah.
Like to do it. Uh, who all did you get offers from? What were some of the different people?

I got an offer from Earl Heinz. Who want me to come up? Uh. Yeah. Got off. Uh. Oliver wanted me to come up there with him. I wouldn't leave though. And then we had this fellow, Fat Wallace. He wanted me to come up with him. But I wasn't going no way.
Well, how did Fat Wallace know you? Fat used to come down here often.
Yeah, Fat used to come here to the Lyric Theater. When I was waiting for Beansy. Sure, Fat used to come over there and sit in and play with us a lot of times.
This was at the E-line.
Yeah.
Yeah, he used to come in there a lot of times. But was he good in a band?
Yeah, he had a band.
I mean as a band piano player, when he played with the Auditor. Sure.
Fine, fine.
Yeah, he was a fine man in a band.

Matter of fact, he had a good band. Yeah, I think he had six pieces there, it was wonderful. Because they used to come down here often, they'd play on the stage, you know. Of course he'd do his acting and things like that. But come down to the actual playing, he could play a lot of piano. Fat was a good musician. He'd just do that clowning and singing and going. But he could play nothing. Sit outside and think he couldn't play. Play a lot of piano. Often wondering why the youngsters these days don't like to play the type of music that we played years ago. All they want to play is rock and roll. And if you take that away from them, they can't even feel their home. I remember, you know, it was about four months ago. A trumpet player of ours got sick out there in Bay St. Louis. And went and got one of the little rock and roll trumpet players. And that guy come in there playing. He was trying to play this progressive music. Running all over his home. Kind of like a run over boat running. Running so far out of the key. I thought he was going overboard that war. Couldn't play a waltz. Play a waltz and he have to hold his hand, hold his horn in his hand. Listen. Couldn't get in there. If he got in there, he wanted to play that. Oh Lord.
There you go again. Could he hold a note and get a tone out?

If he could, he didn't. Everything he played was running. He was gone. Now, he was with a good band. The, what they call them? Good rockers. They do a lot of work over there on that coach. A lot of work. But it's nothing but that rock and roll. And if you get him out of that, you can't play nothing. And not only him, it's a gang of them like that. They got a gang of them right around here like that. You take them out of that rock and roll band and you won't hear nothing in the world they can play. And I don't know why. I don't know why. This boy. Now, them poach used to be like that. Yeah, them poach used to run. And on from, I don't know what. What he be making and how he be making it. I know he used to be like that. He got so, with nobody iron, you see where he playing now. He coming right on down with that Dixieland. And he's a fine trumpet player. But he used to play all that stuff. And he swore he was going to never play Dixieland. Playing it today. If he want to work, he going to play it.
I was wondering about some of the bands you heard when you were a kid. When you were very young, before you even started playing. Do you remember any other than your father's band?

I mentioned the few I heard. As a matter of fact, I heard practically all of them because they used to come out there on that coast. Such as Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, Riddick, Riddick, Riddick, Punch Miller. Uh, a band used to come out there called the Maple Leaf Band. That was with, uh, Freddie Kepert. He used to lead that band. And all those boys used to come out there. I used to hear them. Matter of fact, they used to have what you call a trolley ride from Biloxi to Peskristad. It hooked five or six, uh, trolley cars together. Like an excursion train. And they'd come down there. Oh, they'd have eight or nine hundred of them on there. They'd come down there. They used to have a place there called a profillion. Just the top on it and the floor, no sides. And, uh, summer place, you know. And they'd come down there, dance for four hours. And a trolley car would pull right back up in front of the place. And, uh, everybody would load up on their trolley car. And go on back to Biloxi. Or either they would leave Biloxi some, one time and then go, I mean, leave Peskristad and go to Biloxi. And, uh, my daddy used to play a lot of them. Then he used to get, a lot of time he used to get savvy. It's different bands he used to get.
Who was in your daddy's band? Did he have a band of his own or what?

Yeah, he had a band of his own. He had a fellow by the name of Joe Davis playing guitar. A fellow by the name of Selby Thomas on, uh, bass. Uh, uh, what's his trumpet player name? Uh, Moulier Melanson. He was on trumpet. And, uh, I was on drums. My cousin was playing drums before. I got big enough to play drums. And his name? Charlie Watson. And, uh, who else? At that time, they wasn't usually getting, I mean, no piano. And then... Trombone? Well, trombone and a fellow by the name of, uh, Frank Toes playing trombone.

As a matter of fact, his son's playing trombone somewhere around Memphis. Do you know his son's name? They call him Wash. I don't know his other name. All I know is Wash. Did you name a clarinet player with your father's family? No. No, he didn't have one?
No, he did.

He had a fallout of Basin who used to call Summer of the Bot. Used to play with him a lot. He had another fallout of Basin who used to play with him too, but I forget his name. They used to do the Ice Wake that one. I remember when he was playing at the Great Southern Hotel there in Gulfport. Playing out there on Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and Sundays. And they was making around $35, $40 a week. And that was pretty good money in them days. Yeah, it was a nice having those days.
Were they a straight reading band or were they ragtime style or?

No, just ragtime style. Nobody in the band read at that time. Some of them read a little, but it was about the best musician they had in there. They had the clarinet player. But none of the rest of them didn't read note one. They got together and got to play it, that's all.
Well, how long do you think they'd been playing ragtime or jazz? Could you judge?
Oh, ragtime music's been here, I guess, since around 86. They even have a ragtime music. As a matter of fact, I heard a record my daddy had around home there. Was made in 86.

segments.title: Personnel of the La Vida band
segments.summary: Handy lists the men who worked with him at the La Vida, including Lee Collins, the Marrero brothers, Roy Evans and Jim Robinson.

segments.title: Years at La Vida, Golden Dragon and the Pelican
segments.summary: Handy dates his time at La Vida to about 1926-30 and says he organized a large orchestra for the Golden Dragon and the Pelican.

segments.title: Old man Kimball on bass
segments.summary: Handy names Kimball as his bassist and the interviewer confirms he is the father of a bassist who played with Celestin.

segments.title: St. Louis: Democratic Club and 34 East Market
segments.summary: After the Pelican Handy goes to St. Louis, plays the Democratic Club and 34 East Market, and meets Guy Kelly, Walter Barnes' band and the Jeter-Pillars band.

segments.title: St. Louis sidemen, Sleepy's trumpet surprise, illness and Springfield
segments.summary: Handy recalls New Orleans men in St. Louis, the second trumpeter who outplayed Guy Kelly, his illness in hospital around 1938-39, and a small band in Springfield.

segments.title: Springfield band, the drunken pianist, Don Albert and Kid Rena's trick
segments.summary: Handy describes his Springfield band, a brilliant piano player who was always drunk, seeing Don Albert, and being tripped up by Kid Rena at the fairgrounds.

segments.title: Clarinetists Zeb and Watson; the band at Pete Herman's
segments.summary: Handy praises the clarinetists Zeb and Watson, then lists the band he had at Pete Herman's with Ridgely, Shots and Emma Barrett.

segments.title: Earl Trusclair teaches saxophone fingering; end of Pete Herman's job
segments.summary: Earl Trusclair showed Handy saxophone fingering in exchange for clarinet fingering; the Pete Herman's job lasted about a year before Ridgely broke up the band.

segments.title: Charlie Parker and hidden listeners such as Earl Bostic
segments.summary: Handy never knew Charlie Parker but says many players, including Earl Bostic, hung around to listen to him; he also remembers Joe Harris.

segments.chapter: Offers, Earl Foster and Fats Waller
segments.title: Earl Foster's band and falling asleep at the drums
segments.summary: Handy recalls Earl Foster and Kaiser at Cornell and Burgundy, where Foster fell asleep playing drums while Handy filled in.

segments.chapter: Offers, Earl Foster and Fats Waller
segments.title: Offers to leave town: telegrams, Earl Hines, Oliver, Fats Waller
segments.summary: Handy says he turned down offers from Earl Hines, Oliver and Fats Waller, and stayed after marriage and his first child; he has old telegrams at home.

segments.chapter: Offers, Earl Foster and Fats Waller
segments.title: Fats Waller at the Lyric Theater and as a pianist
segments.summary: Fats came to the Lyric Theater and sat in; Handy says he had a good six-piece band and played much real piano behind the clowning, then turns to young players.

segments.chapter: Offers, Earl Foster and Fats Waller
segments.title: Rock and roll trumpeters cannot play real music
segments.summary: Handy complains that young rock and roll players cannot hold a note, play a waltz or play outside their style.

segments.title: Bands heard as a boy on the Mississippi coast
segments.summary: Handy recalls hearing Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, Punch Miller and the Maple Leaf Band, and the trolley excursions from Biloxi.

segments.title: His father's band and its members
segments.summary: Handy names the men in his father's band, himself on drums, and its Gulfport hotel job paying $35-40 a week.

segments.title: Ragtime style and reading in the early band
segments.summary: The early band played ragtime by ear, with only the clarinetist reading; Handy says ragtime was around since about 1886 and recalls a record his father owned.
